summary:
Delhi stands under India's national framework. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme.

Human Rights Watch reported on 26 March 2026 that the bill removes the right to self-identification, limits recognition to those groups and intersex people, mandates medical certification, and creates offences of coercing or alluring a person that could criminalise the support systems trans people rely on. Human Rights Watch calls the bill a major reversal of hard-won rights and has urged the president not to sign it.

BBC News reported that the amendment bill has cleared both houses of Parliament and awaits presidential assent, reversing the 2014 Supreme Court ruling that established self-identification. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel has asked the government to reconsider, citing privacy and dignity concerns. The government argues the narrower definition will make welfare benefits, job reservations and healthcare support more targeted while strengthening protections against exploitation and trafficking.

India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, but only about 32,500 hold the identity cards essential for accessing social security. This documentation gap bears on visitors and residents in Delhi alike, the capital, and the sources record no Delhi-specific enforcement event.

Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has held covers gender identity and sexual orientation under Article 15. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024: replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
tangentialFactors:
Delhi's status as the national capital concentrates the checkpoint and documentation risks seen elsewhere in India: airports, railway stations and central security forces have all featured in reported incidents involving trans persons, and the same agencies operate in Delhi.

Activist Grace Banu told a Delhi press conference that the community sought "recognition without invasion" and "rights without humiliation", indicating that the capital is a site of organised advocacy as well as of contested enforcement.

The Supreme Court's advisory panel review and the pending presidential assent mean the recognition regime in force in Delhi could still change; the 2014 NALSA position and the 2018 decriminalisation ruling remain the reference points being contested.

Compared with states running active transgender welfare boards such as Tamil Nadu and Kerala, Delhi's own welfare delivery for trans residents is not described in these sources, so visitors should not assume board-style entitlements apply in the capital.
localsOnly:
Delhi residents who are trans, non-binary or gender-fluid may fall outside the amended recognition scheme if they self-identify outside the hijra, kinner or intersex categories, which affects access to identity cards and the welfare schemes tied to them.

Nationally only about 32,500 of the 487,803 transgender persons recorded in the last census hold identity cards, so documentation gaps affect residents as well as visitors seeking to prove status.

The Ayushman Bharat expansion of April 2024 covers transition-related healthcare for transgender people, and the August 2024 Ministry of Finance clarification removes restrictions on joint bank accounts and partner beneficiary designations for LGBTQ people.

The Madras High Court's 2021 S. Sushma guidelines and the National Medical Commission's 2022 conversion-therapy ban are national in reach, though clandestine conversion-therapy networks continue to operate.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not record any Delhi-specific enforcement incident under the 2026 amendment; the documentation and checkpoint cases cited come from Allahabad High Court, Chennai, Kolkata and Assam, and their application to Delhi is inferred from the national pattern rather than directly sourced.

Delhi's own transgender welfare board, housing subsidies or state-level surgery provisions are not described in the inventory, so the capital's resident-facing entitlements beyond the national Ayushman Bharat scheme remain unresolved.

Whether the president signs the amendment bill, and how the Supreme Court advisory panel's reconsideration request is answered, are open questions at the time of these sources.

The scale of clandestine conversion-therapy activity after the 2021 and 2022 bans is not quantified in the inventory.
